A_target.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Bipartite Graph|bipartite graph]] with parts $X$ and $Y$.
Then $G$ has a [[Definition:Matching (Graph Theory)|matching]] saturating $X$ {{iff}}:
:$\forall S \subseteq X: \card {\map N S} \ge \card S$
where $\map N S$ is the set of [[Definition:Neighborhood (Graph Theory)|neighbours]] of $S$.

B_source.statement: To prove a statement for all finite instances, suppose there is a counterexample, take one minimal with respect to some measure, and construct from it a strictly smaller counterexample.

substitutions.the measure being minimized: the number of vertices on the saturated side
substitutions.the case split on the minimal counterexa: whether some proper nonempty subset has exactly as many neighbours as elements
substitutions.the smaller instance produced: one of the two subgraphs obtained by splitting at that tight set

derived.the contradiction with minimality: both smaller pieces satisfy the neighbour condition and so have matchings
derived.combining the smaller solutions: the two matchings union to a saturating matching of the original

validity_conditions: If no proper nonempty subset is tight, removing any single matched pair leaves the condition intact with slack, giving a smaller instance directly.
If some proper nonempty subset is tight, splitting at it produces two instances, and the neighbour condition must be verified separately on each, using tightness for the outside part.
Both pieces are strictly smaller, so minimality of the counterexample is contradicted in either case.
proof_plan:
The condition is clearly necessary.
{{AimForCont}} the condition holds but $G$ is a counterexample with $\card X$ minimal.

Case 1: $\card {\map N S} \ge \card S + 1$ for every non-empty proper $S \subsetneq X$.
Case 2: $\card {\map N S} = \card S$ for some non-empty proper $S \subsetneq X$.

In Case 1, match any $x \in X$ to a neighbour $y$, and delete both; the remaining graph still satisfies the condition and has smaller $X$.
In Case 2, the graphs induced on $S \cup \map N S$ and on $\paren {X \setminus S} \cup \paren {Y \setminus \map N S}$ both satisfy the condition and have smaller $X$.

By minimality, each smaller instance has a saturating matching.
Combining them gives a matching saturating $X$, a contradiction.
This proves [[Hall's Marriage Theorem]].
{{qed}}
